title: Review a React context used for rapidly changing server state
description: Problem: Review a React context used for rapidly changing server state. Solve this problem with multiple approaches and detailed explanations.

data.text: **Review a React context used for rapidly changing server state** is a state-architecture smell. React Context broadcasts any value change to every consumer, regardless of whether they care about that specific update. When the value is server state that updates frequently—API responses, WebSocket messages, or polling data—every consumer re-renders on every tick, even if its branch of the tree does not use the changed data.
Why Context is a poor fit for server state

items: Context triggers re-renders for every consumer when the value reference changes, even if the consumer uses memoization
Server state updates on a timer (polling, SSE, WebSocket) can fire dozens of times per minute
Merging server state into a single context value creates a single point of update with a large blast radius
Context does not provide caching, deduplication, or background refetching
Caching and invalidation logic must be written by hand, often incorrectly
Testing requires wrapping every test in the full provider tree

terms.definition: Data that lives on the server and is fetched over the network. It is inherently asynchronous and can become stale.
Data that lives in the browser and is local to the app: UI toggles, form inputs, modal open flags.
A caching strategy that returns cached data immediately while refreshing it in the background.
Marking cached data as outdated so it is refetched on the next read.
The number of components that must re-render when a piece of state changes.

data.text: The typical anti-pattern is a single ApiContext that stores the entire server state tree. A polling interval updates the context every five seconds, and every component that calls useContext(ApiContext) re-renders even if it only reads user.profile while the update changed user.notifications.

data.title: Context for rapidly changing server state
data.content: This pattern causes every consumer to re-render on every poll, even if their slice of state did not change:

items: React Query / TanStack Query: per-query caching, background refetching, and selective subscriptions
Zustand with selectors: components subscribe to slices of state and only re-render when their slice changes
Split contexts: separate UserContext, PostsContext, and NotificationsContext so updates are scoped
Event-driven updates: dispatch fine-grained events to individual stores instead of broadcasting a monolithic state
URL state: cacheable and shareable server state can live in the URL via query parameters

cards.title: Single Context
cards.description: One context holds all server state and updates on a timer.
cons: All consumers re-render on every update

cards.title: React Query
cards.description: Per-query cache with background refetching and stale-while-revalidate.

cards.title: Split Contexts
cards.description: Multiple small contexts, each managing its own domain of server state.
cons: Still no caching or refetch logic

cards.title: Zustand with selectors
cards.description: Global store where components subscribe to specific slices.

data.title: Separate client state from server state
data.text: Client state is UI toggles, form inputs, and local selections. Server state is data that originated on the server and can become stale. Treat them with different tools. Context is fine for client state; use React Query or a dedicated server-state library for data that changes on a schedule.

items: Identify the server-state queries currently in Context
Install React Query and create query hooks for each endpoint
Replace useContext reads with useQuery calls in the components that need them
Remove the ApiContext provider and related polling effect
Verify render counts with React DevTools Profiler

data.title: Migrate server state out of Context
data.description: Take a component that reads server state from a single Context. Migrate it to React Query with per-query hooks. Measure render counts before and after.
steps: Identify the Context value and how often it updates
Create a useQuery hook for the specific endpoint the component needs
Replace the useContext call with the query hook
Remove the component from the Context consumer list
Profile render counts in React DevTools to confirm the reduction
data.expectedOutcome: The component should re-render only when its specific query data changes, not on every global state update.

items.question: Is Context always wrong for server state?
items.answer: Context is fine for server state that changes rarely, like feature flags or user profile. It becomes a problem when the value updates frequently and many consumers do not need every update.

items.question: What about WebSocket messages?
items.answer: WebSocket data is ideal for React Query with a custom query function that returns a promise resolving on the next message. Alternatively, use a Zustand store with a selector so each component subscribes to the channel it cares about.

items.question: Can I use Context for server state if I memoize the value?
items.answer: Memoizing the value object only prevents re-renders when the reference is stable. If the inner data changes, you still need to create a new reference, which triggers all consumers. Memoization does not solve the broadcast problem.

data.title: Summary
points: Context broadcasts changes to every consumer, regardless of whether they use the changed data
Use React Query or per-query hooks for server state that updates frequently
Split large contexts into domain-specific ones if you must use Context
Measure render counts before and after to verify the improvement
Keep client state and server state in separate tools
data.takeaway: The right tool for server state is one that knows about caching, staleness, and background refetching. Context is not that tool.
